script.title: Your first year freelancing: the complete money setup
script.hook: Going freelance changes three things at once: how you get paid, how you pay tax, and how you save for later. Nobody hands you a checklist, so here's one. We'll go in the order you should actually do it, with real twenty twenty-six numbers, and by the end you'll have a system that runs in about an hour a month. Quick note: this is education, not tax advice, and state rules vary.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Going freelance changes three things at once: how you get paid, how you pay tax, and how you save for later. Nobody hands you a checklist, so here's one. We'll go in the order you should actually do it, with real twenty twenty-six numbers, and by the end you'll have a system that runs in about an hour a month. Quick note: this is education, not tax advice, and state rules vary.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes standing at the start of a winding path with seven stepping stones. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Paperwork
segments.narration: Step one is ten minutes of paperwork. Get a free Employer Identification Number on irs.gov. As a sole proprietor you don't need one, but it lets you put the EIN on client W-9 forms instead of your Social Security number. Never pay a website to get it for you. You also don't need an LLC to start. Plenty of freelancers begin as sole proprietors and decide on an LLC later, for liability reasons, not taxes.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. an ID card with a padlock next to a small form. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Accounts
segments.narration: Step two: separate the money. Open a business-only checking account for client payments and business costs, and a separate savings account for taxes. Then pay yourself from business checking to personal on a schedule, like a paycheck, every two weeks. Leave a buffer in the business account for slow months. Look for no monthly fees and FDIC insurance, and if it's an app, check which partner bank actually holds the money.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three small vaults in a row connected by arrows. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Business budget
segments.narration: Before the tax percentage, one more account decision: how much buffer to keep in the business account. Freelance income arrives in lumps, and the gap between finishing work and getting paid is often thirty to sixty days. A buffer of one to two months of your own paychecks, plus a month of business costs, lets you keep paying yourself the same amount even when a client is late. Build it slowly from your first few payments. It's the difference between a steady paycheck and a stressful one.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small reservoir feeding a steady stream. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Set-aside
segments.narration: Step three: decide your tax set-aside. Clients don't withhold anything, so the day a payment lands, move a fixed percentage to tax savings. Twenty-five to thirty percent is a common starting point. Here's why. At sixty thousand of net profit, a single filer owes about twelve thousand in federal tax in twenty twenty-six: about eight and a half thousand in self-employment tax and about three and a half thousand in income tax. That's twenty percent, before state tax. Thirty percent covers most states with room to spare.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin stack being split with a coral slice going into a vault. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Records
segments.narration: Step four: records. Keep an income log with every payment, client, date and amount, because many clients won't send a 1099 at all. For payments made in twenty twenty-six, a 1099-NEC is generally only required once a client pays you two thousand dollars. Keep receipts for expenses, a mileage log written the same day you drive, and a photo of your home office if you use one. Ten minutes a month labelling your bank statement is enough.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a tidy grid of rows next to a small receipt box. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Pricing
segments.narration: Before taxes get complicated, a word about your rate, because it determines everything else. Your rate has to cover what an employer used to pay for: both halves of Social Security and Medicare, health insurance, retirement, paid time off, and the hours you spend selling and doing admin. A common mistake is taking your old salary, dividing by two thousand hours and charging that. Most freelancers bill far fewer hours than that, so the rate needs to be much higher. Work it out from what you want to take home, not from what others charge.
segments.on_screen_text: Your rate must cover what an employer paid
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a price tag stretched to cover several small icons. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Quarterly
segments.narration: Step five: quarterly estimated taxes. If you expect to owe a thousand dollars or more when you file, you're expected to pay during the year, on April fifteenth, June fifteenth, September fifteenth and January fifteenth. The simplest way to avoid the underpayment penalty is the safe harbor: pay a quarter of last year's total tax at each deadline, or a hundred and ten percent of it if last year's adjusted gross income was over a hundred and fifty thousand. In your first year, when last year had little self-employment income, the safe harbor might be small, so keep saving your percentage too.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four calendar pages along a path. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: First payment
segments.narration: Here's what your first quarterly payment might look like. Say you started freelancing in March and expect forty thousand of profit this year, and last year you were an employee with all your tax withheld. Your safe harbor is last year's total tax, say four thousand dollars, so paying a thousand by each deadline generally protects you from the penalty. But your real bill this year might be around seven thousand four hundred federal. So pay your safe harbor amounts on time, and keep saving your full percentage for April.

segments.heading: Deductions
segments.narration: Step six: deductions. Self-employment tax and income tax are both figured on profit, so every legitimate business expense matters. Common ones are software, equipment, a home office used regularly and exclusively for work, business mileage, professional fees, and payment processing fees. Mixed-use costs like your phone count only for the business share. The test is ordinary and necessary, with a receipt. Skip anything you couldn't explain calmly to an auditor.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a receipt passing through a simple checkmark gate. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Retirement
segments.narration: Step seven: retirement. You have no employer plan, but you have better tools. A SEP IRA lets you put away about twenty percent of your profit after half of self-employment tax. A Solo 401(k) adds an employee contribution of up to twenty-four thousand five hundred for twenty twenty-six on top of that. At sixty thousand of profit, that's roughly eleven thousand for a SEP or up to about thirty-five thousand for a Solo 401(k). Even a small, automatic monthly contribution counts.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two plant pots growing from coin jars. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Insurance
segments.narration: While you're thinking about protection, consider business insurance. Professional liability, sometimes called errors and omissions, covers claims that your work caused a client a loss. General liability covers injuries or damage if you work at a client's site or they visit you. Some clients require one or both in their contracts. Policies for solo freelancers are often affordable, and the premiums are a business expense. An LLC doesn't replace this; insurance is what actually pays when something goes wrong.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a shield over a small laptop. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Health
segments.narration: Step eight: health. If you buy your own marketplace insurance and aren't eligible for an employer plan, including a spouse's, your premiums are generally deductible. And from twenty twenty-six, bronze and catastrophic marketplace plans are treated as HSA-compatible, so you may be able to open a health savings account and contribute up to forty-four hundred dollars for self-only coverage. Confirm your plan qualifies first.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a simple shield with a medical cross next to a small vault. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Getting paid
segments.narration: Step nine: get paid on time. Use a short contract with scope, price, a deposit, and late terms. Put a real due date on every invoice, add a pay-now link, and send a friendly reminder three days before it's due. Cash flow is the thing that actually ends freelance careers, so this matters as much as tax.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. an invoice with a big friendly button and a calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Year one traps
segments.narration: Let's name the year-one traps, so you can step around them. Spending the tax money because it was sitting in the same account. Underpricing because the first client set the rate. Saying yes to every project with no contract. Waiting until April to discover you owe twelve thousand dollars. And not keeping records, then guessing at deductions. Every step in this video exists to prevent one of these. If you only do three things, separate the accounts, set aside a percentage on the day you're paid, and keep an income log.

script.title: Quarterly estimated taxes, explained with one real-numbers year
script.hook: If you freelance, the IRS expects to be paid four times a year, not once in April. Most first-year freelancers find this out the hard way, with a bill and a penalty. So let's walk one fictional freelancer, Sam, through a whole year with real twenty twenty-six numbers. Education only, not tax advice. We'll cover who has to pay, how Sam's tax is figured, the two ways to choose a payment, how the year plays out, how to pay, lumpy and falling income, filing time, having a job as well, and the mistakes to avoid.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: If you freelance, the IRS expects to be paid four times a year, not once in April. Most first-year freelancers find this out the hard way, with a bill and a penalty. So let's walk one fictional freelancer, Sam, through a whole year with real twenty twenty-six numbers. Education only, not tax advice. We'll cover who has to pay, how Sam's tax is figured, the two ways to choose a payment, how the year plays out, how to pay, lumpy and falling income, filing time, having a job as well, and the mistakes to avoid.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes next to a long timeline with four coral markers. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why quarterly
segments.narration: The US tax system is pay as you go. Employees pay through withholding on every check. Freelancers have no withholding, so they're expected to make estimated payments. If you expect to owe a thousand dollars or more when you file, you generally need to pay along the way, or you can owe an underpayment penalty, which works like interest on the amount that was late.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a paycheck with a withholding box next to a calendar with four dots. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Who owes
segments.narration: First, who actually has to make these payments? Generally, anyone who expects to owe at least a thousand dollars of federal tax for the year after subtracting withholding and refundable credits. That includes freelancers, gig workers, creators with sponsorships, landlords, and people with big investment gains. If you also have a job, you can sometimes cover your freelance tax by increasing your withholding at work instead, because withholding counts as if it were paid evenly through the year. Your state may have its own threshold and rules.
segments.on_screen_text: Owe $1,000+? You likely need to pay
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small threshold line with coins above it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Meet Sam
segments.narration: Sam is a single freelance designer. Last year Sam had a salaried job, with total federal tax of six thousand five hundred dollars. This year Sam goes freelance and expects about sixty thousand of profit. Sam has no other income.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a simple faceless character silhouette at a drawing desk. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What Sam owes
segments.narration: At sixty thousand of profit, Sam's twenty twenty-six federal tax is about twelve thousand thirty-seven dollars. About eight thousand four hundred seventy-eight is self-employment tax, fifteen point three percent on ninety-two point three five percent of profit. About three thousand five hundred fifty-nine is income tax, after half the self-employment tax, the sixteen thousand one hundred standard deduction, and the qualified business income deduction.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two stacked coin piles, the lower one larger. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Two ways
segments.narration: Sam has two ways to decide each payment. Option one: the current-year method, pay ninety percent of this year's tax in four parts. That's about twenty-seven hundred a quarter. Option two: the safe harbor, pay a hundred percent of last year's total tax. Last year was six thousand five hundred, so that's one thousand six hundred twenty-five a quarter.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two paths splitting from one point. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Sam's year
segments.narration: Here's how Sam's year actually plays out. In April, Sam pays sixteen twenty-five and has about four thousand five hundred in tax savings, because thirty percent of the first months' income went straight there. In June, another sixteen twenty-five. A big project lands in the summer, so in September Sam pays sixteen twenty-five again, and the tax savings account keeps growing. In January, Sam pays the last sixteen twenty-five. That's sixty-five hundred paid, and the savings account holds more than enough for the April balance.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a timeline with four coins and a growing vault. No text, no logos, no real people.

chart.title: Sam's payments, running total
chart.note: Safe harbor: 100% of last year's $6,500 tax, in four equal payments.

segments.heading: Sam's choice
segments.narration: Sam picks the safe harbor, because last year's number is known and it generally protects against the penalty even if this year's income jumps. But Sam keeps setting aside thirty percent of every payment, because the remaining balance, about fifty-five hundred dollars, is still due in April.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small boat in a harbor and a vault filling beside it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The dates
segments.narration: Sam's payments are due April fifteenth, June fifteenth, September fifteenth, and January fifteenth of the next year. The quarters are uneven: June's payment covers just April and May. Dates that land on a weekend or holiday move to the next business day.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four calendar pages spaced unevenly. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Wrong year
segments.narration: One mistake to avoid when paying: choosing the wrong tax year. The January payment is for the previous year, even though you're paying in the new year. If you pick the wrong year, the money sits on the wrong account, and you may get a penalty notice for the year that looks short. If it happens, contact the IRS to move the payment. And always keep the confirmation numbers in one place, because you'll need the totals and dates when you file.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a dropdown menu with the previous year highlighted. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How to pay
segments.narration: To pay, Sam uses IRS Direct Pay, or signs in to an IRS online account, and picks estimated tax for the right year. It takes about five minutes. Sam saves each confirmation number. Paying by debit or credit card works too, but processors charge a fee. Sam's state has an income tax, so Sam makes state estimated payments on its own schedule.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a laptop with a check mark and a small state outline. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If Sam's income fell
segments.narration: What if Sam's income had dropped instead? Say Sam only earned twenty thousand this year. The tax would be about three thousand. Ninety percent of that is about twenty-seven hundred, much less than last year's six thousand five hundred. In that case the current-year method is the better choice, and Sam could pay around six hundred eighty a quarter. The rule is: you can pay the smaller of the two, as long as you estimate honestly. Recheck mid-year so you're not overpaying.
segments.on_screen_text: Income fell? Current-year may be smaller
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a down arrow next to two coin stacks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Lumpy income
segments.narration: What if income is lumpy, with a big project in the fall? The annualized installment method on Form 2210 lets you match payments to when you actually earned the money. It's more paperwork, and tax software can do it. If you missed a payment, pay as soon as you can. The penalty grows with time, so late is better than never.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a bumpy line chart with steps beneath it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Filing
segments.narration: When Sam files in the spring, the four estimated payments are listed on the return as payments already made, just like withholding for an employee. The return compares the total tax with everything paid. Sam owes the difference, about fifty-five hundred, which comes straight from the tax savings account. If Sam had paid more than the total, the extra would come back as a refund, or Sam could apply it to next year's first estimated payment.
segments.on_screen_text: Filing: payments made vs total tax
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a balance scale with coins on both sides. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Year two
segments.narration: In year two, Sam's safe harbor becomes this year's full twelve thousand thirty-seven. If Sam's adjusted gross income ever goes above a hundred and fifty thousand, the safe harbor becomes a hundred and ten percent. Each April, update the number.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar page turning to a new year. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: W-2 too
segments.narration: A quick note if you have a job as well. Your employer withholds tax from your salary based on your W-4. Freelance profit on top of that is taxed at your highest bracket, plus self-employment tax, and nothing is withheld for it. You can make estimated payments, or you can ask your employer to withhold more through a new W-4, which is often easier. Either way, check your numbers mid-year with the IRS withholding estimator or a calculator.
segments.on_screen_text: Got a job too? Raise withholding
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a briefcase and a small coin stack side by side. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: System
segments.narration: Sam's whole system: a business account, a tax savings account with thirty percent of every payment, four calendar reminders a week before each deadline, and ten minutes a month to check the tax account is on track. The Quarterly Tax Tracker in the description does Sam's math for you: income log, expenses, safe harbor and the current-year estimate side by side.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes relaxing beside four ticked calendar pages. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mistakes
segments.narration: Let's finish with the five most common estimated tax mistakes. Not paying at all in year one. Paying the safe harbor and spending the rest of the set-aside, then being short in April. Choosing the wrong tax year online. Forgetting the state. And waiting until a payment is months late before paying. Every one of these is avoidable with the system we just walked through: a tax account, a percentage, four reminders and a monthly check-in.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. five small crossed-out icons in a row. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap: you pay four times a year if you'll owe a thousand or more. Use the safe harbor for peace of mind, keep saving your percentage for the April balance, pay on IRS Direct Pay, and don't forget your state. Put the four dates in your calendar today with a reminder a week before each, and the whole thing takes about an hour a year. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.
